name: Chujohime Seigan Zakura
species: Yamazakura Cherry, rare double-flowered cultivar (Prunus jamasakura / Prunus itosakura)
access: Free, temple grounds open 9:00-17:00 daily; bus B74 from JR Gifu Station or Meitetsu Gifu Station to Korin Park entrance, then approx. 10 min walk
transport: Bus B74 from JR Gifu Station (about 45 min, then 10 min walk)
story:
In 2008 a few hundred of this tree's seeds spent eight months aboard the International Space Station. They went up with seeds from fourteen famous Japanese trees, and this one had more riding on it than most: until then, grafting had been the only reliable way to make another. At least one of the returned seeds germinated, grew and eventually flowered, which was reported in Japan as a small sensation.

The reason for the fuss is the flower. An ordinary yamazakura opens five petals. This one opens twenty to thirty, pale pink and doubled, and no other tree of the cultivar is known to exist. Japan made it a National Natural Monument on 2 April 1929.

Its age is a story rather than a measurement. By tradition the Nara-period princess Chujohime, fleeing her stepmother's persecution, was healed after praying to Kannon here at Ganjo-ji and planted the cherry in gratitude. That legend is where the figure of roughly 1,200 years comes from. Nobody has dated the wood.

The trunk is an open question too. The city of Gifu records the tree at about nine metres tall with a trunk 31 centimetres through at chest height; a travel guide gives 8.1 metres and a full metre and a half. Those cannot both be right, so we quote neither as fact. What both agree on is that this is a slender tree for its reputation, kept going by careful hands rather than by bulk.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the flowers, twenty to thirty pale pink petals where every other mountain cherry opens five. It stands in the grounds of Ganjo-ji, slim and eight or nine metres tall rather than thick-trunked.

best_time.label: early April, when the doubled flowers open, twenty to thirty petals apiece instead of the usual five

name: Daio-sugi (Yakushima)

location.address: Ooyama Trail, en route to Jomon Sugi, Yakushima, Kumage District, Kagoshima Prefecture

access: Free, but reached only by a strenuous hike (about 4-5 hours one way from the Arakawa trailhead along the old tram road and Ooyama Trail) inside Yakushima's protected forest, part of the standard route to Jomon Sugi; the trailhead itself requires a pre-booked shuttle bus during peak season because private cars are restricted
transport: Shuttle bus from Yakushima's Miyanoura/Anbo area to the Arakawa trailhead, then hike (~4h to Ooyama Trail entrance, ~45 min further to the tree)
story:
For a while this was the largest cedar anybody knew of on Yakushima. Then Jomon Sugi was found and named, and the Daio-sugi dropped to second, which is not a demotion you feel standing under it. Japan's Ministry of the Environment measures it at 11.1 metres around at chest height and 24.7 metres tall, on a slope roughly 1,200 metres up in the island's interior forest. That is a trunk about the width of a small room.

The same ministry gives its age as more than 3,000 years. That is the government's own broad estimate rather than a ring count, and the phrasing matters: it is a floor, not a ceiling. A cedar standing here that long was already old before anything about Japan was written down.

Getting there is the price and most of the point. The tree stands directly on the marked trail to Jomon Sugi, inside a World Heritage core zone, about four hours from the Arakawa trailhead along an old logging tram road and another forty-five minutes up the Ooyama Trail. Private cars cannot reach the trailhead in the busy season, so the day starts with a booked shuttle bus. Then you walk.

Nothing is fenced and nothing is charged. The trail simply passes it, signed, after four hours in which everything else has also been a cedar and none of them has been this one.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the size: 11.1 metres round at chest height and 24.7 metres tall, the largest cedar on the Jomon Sugi route apart from Jomon Sugi itself. It stands signed beside the Ooyama Trail, about 1,200 metres up.

name: The Camphor Tree of Hongo Yumicho
access: Free, stands beside a narrow public road in a dense residential/office block in Hongo; visible and reachable on foot from the street, no parking on site so walking from the station is recommended
transport: 5-10 min walk from Hongo-sanchome Station (Tokyo Metro Marunouchi / Toei Oedo lines), or 6 min from Kasuga Station (Toei Oedo / Mita lines)
story:
The biggest tree in Bunkyo Ward is not in a park. It stands on a narrow street in Hongo, houses and offices tight against it and restaurants across the road: a camphor twenty metres tall with a trunk between 8.4 and 8.5 metres round, depending on which of its two record-keepers you ask. Japanese Wikipedia gives the lower figure, the Bunkyo Tourism Association the higher, and ten centimetres is about what a tape does on a trunk that shape.

Both put it at roughly 600 years, an estimate rather than a planting date. Take it at face value and the tree was already mature before the Tokugawa shoguns made Edo their capital in 1603, and it has watched the block around it be rebuilt more times than anyone has counted.

The names here rhyme in a way nobody arranged. The district was once Goyumi-cho, named for the shogunal archery corps quartered in it, which is why the tree is called the old camphor of Yumicho. The ground later held the residence of the Kaisho family, said to descend from the medieval warrior Kusunoki Masashige, whose name means camphor.

Shiba Ryotaro wrote it into his travel serial Kaido wo Yuku in the early 1990s. Bunkyo Ward lists it as a protected tree, a municipal designation rather than a national one. There is no gate, no fee and nowhere to park: you walk up from Hongo-sanchome and it is simply there, in the way.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about 8.4 metres round and twenty metres tall, easily the largest tree in Bunkyo Ward. It stands directly beside a narrow Hongo street, restaurants opposite, with no park or garden around it.

name: Ibi Nido-zakura (the Ibi Twice-Blooming Cherry)
species: Cherry, a rare two-stage-flowering cultivar (Prunus sp., 'nido-zakura')
age_estimate: not reliably documented; a commonly cited local figure is roughly 140 years for the current above-ground trunk

location.address: 184-1/184-2 Nidozakura, Minamikata, Ono-cho, Ibi-gun, Gifu Prefecture (Nidozakura Park, former Daizo-ji temple site)

access: Free, public park (Nidozakura Park, completed March 2012) built specifically around the designated trees
transport: Bus from JR Ogaki Station to Ono Bus Center, then the town-office-bound bus to the 'Minamikata' stop, short walk from there
story:
This cherry flowers twice without finishing the first flowering. Single blooms open, and as their petals begin to wilt a second flush of buds opens at the centre of the same flower, doubled this time. The habit gave the tree its name, nido-zakura, the twice-blooming cherry, and won it National Natural Monument status on 7 March 1923.

What stands in the park today has survived two deaths. The original grew at Daizo-ji temple with a trunk about three metres round, and a storm brought it down in 1833. A second tree rose from that stump, reached about 1.8 metres round, and died in 1934. Everything flowering here now is shoots off the same root system, which outlived both trunks. In 2009 three of those shoots were added to the 1923 designation, so four trees carry it between them.

Nobody has published an age for the present growth. A figure repeated widely online gives the trunk as 160 centimetres round, eight metres tall and roughly 140 years old, but it appears in no official register, and we would rather say that than quote it as fact. If you know of a dated measurement, tell us.

The town of Ono built the park around the four designated trees in 2012 and has since planted 86 more cherries beside them, every one raised from cuttings off the originals. The rarity is being propagated rather than merely fenced.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the flowers, which open in two stages: single blooms first, then a doubled second flush from the centre of the same flower. It stands in Nidozakura Park with three designated sister trees around it.

best_time.label: early April, when the first petals wilt and a second, doubled flush opens at the centre of the same flower
